**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 113, verses 1–2:**

﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾ ﴿from the evil of what He has created﴾

The command to "say" requires preserving these exact words, because they are the words that Allah specified for the Prophet ﷺ to seek refuge with, so their supplications are hoped to be answered. This recited speech does not contain anything that is imposed as a duty or an action to be performed, so that the meaning would be "say to them such-and-such," as in His saying: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1]. Rather, it is the expression of a meaning in the soul, which these specific words indicate.

It has been narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he asked the Prophet ﷺ about the two refuge-seeking surahs (al-Mu'awwidhatayn), and he said: "It was said to me, 'Say,' so I said [it], so say [it]." He intended by this the preservation of these words for seeking refuge. Since they are from the Qur'an, preserving their wording is obligatory, and seeking refuge is achieved through their meaning and their wording, even through the word "say" itself.

The address in "say" is to the Prophet ﷺ. Since it is Qur'an, the Prophet's ﷺ address with it includes the Ummah, since there is no evidence restricting it to him. For this reason, the Prophet ﷺ commanded some of his Companions to seek refuge with this surah, and for the same reason he used to seek refuge with both surahs for al-Hasan and al-Husayn, as is established in the Sahih. Thus the imperative form directed at the addressee is used in two senses: its being directed at a specific person, which is the basic meaning, and the intention of everyone to whom it is valid to address, which is one of the methods of address whose intended meaning is indicated by contextual clues. So it is an instance of using a homonym (mushtarak, a term carrying more than one meaning) in both of its meanings.

The use of the first-person form in "I seek refuge" follows what is intended by the second-person form in "say." Thus it is commanded for everyone who wishes to seek refuge with them.

As for the recitation of these two surahs by one who recites them over others, as in what is reported: "The Prophet ﷺ used to seek refuge for al-Hasan and al-Husayn with the two Mu'awwidhatayn," and what is reported from 'Aisha, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ used to blow over himself with the refuge-seeking [surahs] during the illness from which he died; when he became heavy, I would blow over him with them and wipe with his own hand for its blessing." This is therefore done with the intention of acting on behalf of one who cannot seek refuge for himself with those words, due to inability, young age, or lack of memorization.

Al-'awdh (seeking refuge) means taking refuge in something that protects the one who seeks it from what he fears. It is said: "'aadha bi-fulan" (he sought refuge with so-and-so), and "'aadha bi-hisn" (he sought refuge in a fortress). It is also said: "ista'adha" when one asks another to grant him protection. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So seek refuge in Allah; indeed, He is the Hearing, the Knowing﴾ [al-A'raf: 200]. And "'aadha min kadha" means he arrived at that which protects him from it. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan﴾ [al-Nahl: 98].

Al-Falaq is the dawn. It is of the form fa'al with the meaning of maf'ul (passive), like al-Samad, because the night is likened to a closed thing from which the dawn splits open. The real meaning of falq is splitting open from the inside of something, and it is used metaphorically (isti'arah) for the appearance of dawn after the darkness of night. This is like the metaphor of bringing out for the appearance of light after darkness, in His saying: ﴿And He darkened its night and brought out its forenoon﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 29], and the metaphor of stripping away for it in His saying: ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip from it the day﴾ [Ya-Sin: 37].

The Lord of the daybreak is Allah, because He is the One who created the causes of the appearance of dawn. The specification of the attribute "Lord of the daybreak" over another attribute is because much evil occurs at night: from thieves, beasts of prey, venomous creatures, the difficulty of travel, the difficulty of rescue, the distance of help, and the intensification of the pains of the sick. So much so that some people of misguidance thought that the night was a god of evil.

The meaning is: "I seek refuge with the Splitter of the dawn as a means of deliverance from the evils of the night, for He is capable of delivering me at night from evil, just as He delivered all the people of the earth by creating the dawn for them." Thus Allah is described by the attribute in which there is a preparation for the answering (of the supplication).

﴿And from the evil of the darkness when it settles﴾

This is the coordination (*'atf*) of specific things that fall within the generality of ﴿from the evil of what He created﴾ [al-Falaq: 2]. They are three kinds of evil:

First, a time in which evil commonly occurs, which is the night.

Second, a class of people whose trade is built on intending harm to others.

Third, a class of people with a disposition that tends to lead them to inflict harm on whoever comes into contact with them.

The phrase ﴿from the evil﴾ [al-Falaq: 2] is repeated after the conjunction particle in this sentence and in the two sentences coordinated with it, even though the conjunction particle suffices without repeating the governing element. This repetition is intended to emphasise the supplication, seeking to make it more likely to be answered. This is a form of entreaty (*ibtihal*), and it suits elaboration (*itnab*).

*Al-ghasiq* describes the night when its darkness becomes intense. It is said: *ghasaqa al-layl yaghsiqu*, meaning the night became dark. God Most High says: ﴿until the darkness of the night﴾ [al-Isra': 78]. So *al-ghasiq* is an adjective of an omitted noun, the omission being clear from the meaning of its description, like *al-jawari* in God's words: ﴿And among His signs are the ships in the sea﴾ [al-Shura: 32]. The indefiniteness of *ghasiq* denotes the class, because what is meant is the class of night.

The indefiniteness of *(ghasiq)* in a context of supplication is intended to convey generality, because the context of supplication calls for generalisation. An example is al-Hariri's words in the Fifth Maqama: "O people of this meaning, may you be protected from harm," meaning, may you be protected from every harm.

The attribution of *al-sharr* (evil) to *ghasiq* is an attribution of a thing to its time, in the sense of (*fi*, "in"), as in God's words: ﴿Rather, it was the plotting of the night and the day﴾ [Saba': 33].

The night is one in which incidents of harm frequently occur, from thieves, predators and vermin, as was mentioned just before.

The restriction of this by the temporal clause ﴿when it settles﴾, that is, when its darkness becomes intense, is because that is the time that rogues, men of corruption and mischief seek out, since heedlessness and sleep are then certain to prevail over people. It is said: *aghdara al-layl*, meaning the night became treacherous, because when its darkness intensifies, treachery increases in it. Thus it is expressed by saying that it is treacherous, by way of rational metaphor (*al-majaz al-'aqli*), meaning that it has become possessed of treachery.

[Page 628]

The meaning of *waqaba* is that it entered and penetrated into a thing. From this comes *al-waqba*, the name for a hollow in a rock where water collects. It is also said *waqabat al-shams*, meaning the sun set. Seeking refuge was specifically tied to the most intense hours of the night, because the harm that is feared is most anticipated then.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 113, verse 4:

﴿And from the evil of those who blow upon knots﴾

This is the second of the special categories that are conjoined to the general phrase in His words: ﴿from the evil of what He created﴾ [al-Falaq: 2]. The conjoining of ﴿the evil of those who blow upon knots﴾ to the evil of the night is because the night is a time when sorcerers seek the opportunity to carry out their witchcraft, so that no one may observe them.

Al-nafth (blowing) is breathing out with movement of the tongue without expelling saliva; it is thus less than al-tafl (spitting). Sorcerers do this when they place the material of their magic on something, tie knots upon it, and then blow upon them.

Thus, by ﴿those who blow upon knots﴾ is meant female sorceresses. The feminine form of the attribute was used because among the Arabs it was generally women who practised magic, since their women had no occupation after preparing the necessities of food, water and cleanliness. Therefore they were much given to such trivialities as magic and soothsaying and the like, so false beliefs spread among them. The Arabs used to claim that the ghoul is a sorceress from the jinn. It is reported in the account of the migration to Abyssinia that 'Imara ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughira was accused of [involvement with] the wife of the Negus, and that the Negus summoned sorceresses for him, and they blew into his urethra, so he became deprived of reason, wandering aimlessly and joining the wild beasts. Al-'Uqad (knots) is the plural of 'uqda, which is a binding in a thread or cord; the sorcerers claim that it is the magic of the bewitched person, which persists as long as that knot remains tied. For this reason they fear its untying, so they bury it or hide it in a place that cannot be found.

God commanded His Messenger ﷺ to seek refuge from the evil of sorcerers, because He guaranteed him that the evil of sorcerers would not reach him. This is a refutation of the claim of the polytheists in their falsehoods that he was bewitched. God says: ﴿And the wrongdoers said, "You follow none but a man bewitched."﴾ [al-Furqan: 8].

The summary here: since the more sound opinion is that the surah is Meccan, the Prophet ﷺ is safe from the evil of those who blow upon knots, because God protected him from them.

As for magic, we have expounded on it at His words: ﴿they taught people magic﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The seeking of refuge was made from those who blow (al-naffathat), not from the act of blowing (al-nafth). He did not say "when they blow upon the knots," to indicate that their blowing upon the knots is not in itself something that brings harm; rather, harm is brought by the blowers, who are engaged in magic. This is because the sorcerer is keen to leave nothing that achieves his aim unattempted; he devises means to deliver it. Perhaps he places in his food or drink substances that corrupt the mind or destroy, intentionally or unintentionally, or filth whose mixing with the body corrupts some elements of the body's regulation, so that its vigour or will is disordered. Perhaps he incites against the victim one who will assassinate him, or one who spies on his circumstances, so as to show those who ask him for magic that his magic does not vary and does not miss.

The definite article in (al-naffathat) is the definite of the genus, and in meaning it is like the indefinite; there is no difference in meaning between it and His words: ﴿from the evil of a darkening night﴾ [al-Falaq: 3] and His words: ﴿from the evil of an envier﴾ [al-Falaq: 5]. The word al-naffathat was preferred in the definite form because definiteness in such a context indicates that it is a reality known to the listener, like the definite form in their saying (arsalaha al-'iraq), as was mentioned earlier at His words: ﴿Praise be to God﴾ [al-Fatihah: 2] in Surat al-Fatihah.

The definite form of (al-naffathat) with the article "al-" indicates that they are known among the Arabs.

[Surah 113, verse 5]

﴿And from the evil of an envier when he envies.﴾

The evil of the envier is conjoined with the evil of the sorcerer, which is itself conjoined with the evil of the night. The connection is direct with the immediately preceding item and indirect with the first item through it. Envy often moves the envier to seek harm for the envied, since he imagines that sorcery removes the blessing he envies. Also, the agitation of the soul (wijdan al-jasad) increases at night, because night is the time of solitude, of the arising of inner thoughts, and of reflection on the circumstances surrounding the envier and the envied.

Envy (hasad) is an inner feeling composed of approving of a blessing in another person together with wishing that it would cease for him, out of jealousy over the other's exclusive possession of that state or over the other's sharing it with the envier. The term hasad may also be used metaphorically for ghibta (admiration/wishing for the like).

[Page 630]

Ghibta (admiration) is a person's wish that he have the same good as someone whose condition pleases him. This is the intended meaning of the authentic hadith: "There is no hasad except in two (matters)," i.e., there is no ghibta, meaning that ghibta is only realized in those two qualities. Shihab al-Din al-Qarafi clarified the difference between hasad and ghibta in the 258th distinction (al-Farq).

Envy may overcome the envier's patience and forbearance, leading him to inflict harm on the envied by destroying the causes of his blessing or by annihilating it entirely. Envy was the first cause of crimes in this world, when one of the two sons of Adam envied his brother because his offering was accepted while the other's was not, as God Most High recounts in Surat al-'Uqud (the Chapter of Covenants).

The restriction of seeking refuge from its evil to the time of ﴿when he envies﴾ is because at that moment he is driven to work evil against the envied, when envy surges within him, and then stratagems and intentions are set in motion to inflict harm upon him. The envy meant in His saying ﴿when he envies﴾ is a particular envy, namely the envy that reaches its fullest reality, so there is no difficulty in restricting envy by the verb (hasada). This is the statement of 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib:

*And Lamis appeared as if she were the full moon of the sky when it shows itself.*

I.e., when it becomes clear and bright.

Since envy necessarily implies that the envied is in a good condition, the Arabs commonly used "the envied" as a metaphor for a chief or noble, and conversely used "the envier" as a metaphor for one in a bad condition. On this is the saying of Abu al-Aswad:

*They envied the young man because they could not attain his efforts, so the people became his enemies and adversaries.*

*Like the co-wives of a beautiful woman who said of her face, out of envy and hatred, "Indeed, it is ill-omened!"*

And the saying of Bashshar ibn Burd:

*If they envy me, I am not one to blame them; before me, people of excellence were envied.*

*So what is with me and with them endures, and most of us die of rage over what he finds.*

**Surat al-Nas (The Chapter of Mankind)**

It was mentioned at the commentary on the first verse of Surat al-Falaq that "the Prophet (ﷺ) named Surat al-Nas (Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind)."

It was also mentioned in Surat al-Falaq that it and Surat al-Nas are called (al-Mu'awwidhatayn, the Two Seeking-Refuge Chapters) and (al-Mushaqshiqatayn), with the shin placed before the qaf. It was also mentioned that al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi stated that they are called (al-Muqashqishatayn), with the two qafs placed before the two shins. Ibn 'Atiyya, in al-Muharrir al-Wajiz, titled it (the second Mu'awwidhah chapter), by making (surah) an idafa to (Mu'awwidhah), as an idafa of a described noun to its descriptor. al-Tirmidhi titled the two (al-Mu'awwidhatayn), and al-Bukhari titled it in his Sahih (the chapter of "Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind").

In our old and modern Maghribi and Mashriqi copies of the Qur'an, this chapter is named (Surat al-Nas), and so are most books of tafsir.

It is Meccan according to those who said Surat al-Falaq is Meccan, and Medinan according to those who said Surat al-Falaq is Medinan. The correct view is that the two were revealed consecutively, so the disagreement regarding one is the same as the disagreement regarding the other.

Al-Suyuti said in al-Itqan that the occasion of revelation was the story of the sorcery of Labid ibn al-A'sam, and that they were revealed together with (Surat al-Falaq). al-Qurtubi and al-Wahidi preceded him in this, and you have already known its refutation in the commentary on Surat al-Falaq.

According to the correct view that it is Meccan, it is counted as the twenty-first of the chapters, revealed after Surat al-Falaq and before Surat al-Ikhlas.

[Page 632]

Its number of verses is six. Al-Suyuti mentioned in al-Itqan an opinion that it has seven verses, but it is not attributed to the scholars of verse counting.

* * *

The Prophet (ﷺ) was guided to seek refuge with God, his Lord, from the evil of the whisperer who tries to corrupt the Prophet's work and his guidance, and who casts into people's souls aversion to his call. In this command there is an indication that God Most High protects him from this, preserving him within himself from the domination of the whisperer's suggestion over him, and completing his call until it spreads among the people. Following this is the teaching of Muslims to seek refuge in the same way, so that they will have from this seeking refuge what is their portion, and from the readiness to be exposed to the whisperer, and from safety from it, according to the degrees of their nearness to God.
